claims.claim: GDP is the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given period.
Only final goods and services are counted; intermediate goods are excluded to avoid double-counting output as it moves through production stages.
The expenditure approach measures GDP = C + I + G + (X - M): consumption, investment, government purchases, and net exports.

Investment (I) means purchases of new capital goods, residential construction, and inventories, not purchases of stocks or bonds; government spending (G) counts federal, state, and local purchases but excludes transfer payments such as Social Security and unemployment benefits; net exports equal exports minus imports.
In 2020, U.S. GDP totaled about $20.9 trillion, with consumption about 67.2%, investment about 17.4%, and government about 18.5% of GDP; on the production side, services were about 60.8%.
Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP is adjusted for inflation using a price index (the GDP deflator), via Real GDP = Nominal GDP / (price index / 100).
GDP per capita is GDP divided by population; using the 2020 figures, about $20.9 trillion over roughly 331 million people is about $63,000 per person.

GDP omits production not exchanged in markets (household and volunteer work) and the informal economy, is only an average that says nothing about inequality, and does not measure leisure, environmental quality, or well-being.

Simon Kuznets built the first U.S. national income accounts (report to the U.S. Senate, National Income 1929-1932, 1934) and cautioned that the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income.
U.S. real GDP increased 2.1 percent for the full year 2025.

sourceRecords.title: What to Know About GDP
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), Learning Center
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports the definition (value of final goods and services produced in the U.S.), the expenditure formula GDP = C + I + G + (X - M), component definitions (investment excludes stocks/bonds; government excludes transfer payments; net exports = exports - imports), the final-vs-intermediate double-counting rule, the nominal (current-dollar) vs real (chained/inflation-adjusted) distinction, and the illustrative 2020 figures (GDP $20.9T; C 67.2%, I 17.4%, G 18.5%; services 60.8%). U.S. government work, public domain; prose written independently.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Macroeconomics 3e, Section 6.2: Adjusting Nominal Values to Real Values
sourceRecords.provider: OpenStax, Rice University (Steven A. Greenlaw, David Shapiro, Daniel MacDonald)

Supports the nominal-vs-real distinction and the conversion Real GDP = Nominal GDP / (price index / 100), including the worked 1960 example ($542.4B, deflator 16.6 -> $3,267.5B in 2012 dollars) and the base-year property that the index equals 100. NC-SA license: reference-only.

sourceRecords.title: Principles of Macroeconomics 3e, Section 6.5: How Well GDP Measures the Well-Being of Society
sourceRecords.provider: OpenStax, Rice University (Steven A. Greenlaw, David Shapiro, Daniel MacDonald)
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports GDP's limitations: excludes non-market production (do-it-yourself work), says nothing about inequality (per capita is only an average), does not capture whether air/water are cleaner or health outcomes improved, ignores leisure/workday length and product variety; and credits Kuznets as the creator of the measurement. NC-SA license: reference-only.

sourceRecords.title: National Income, 1929-1932 (Letter from the Acting Secretary of Commerce transmitting a report prepared by Simon Kuznets), 73rd Congress, 2d Session, Senate Document No. 124
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Senate / U.S. Department of Commerce (Simon Kuznets); digitized by FRASER, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
sourceRecords.notes: Canonical primary source for the origin of U.S. national income accounting and Kuznets' welfare caution ('the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income'). The FRASER PDF returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher; the attribution, title, congressional-report status, and the exact warning sentence were verified via secondary corroboration (World Economic Forum history-of-GDP piece and Wikiquote's sourced Kuznets entry) rather than reproduced from the PDF. U.S. government document, public domain; the one warning phrase is attributed to Kuznets.
